Diagnosis

[S]tudents’ job expectations have changed little and
remain misaligned with actual labour market demands. […]
Students’ career expectations are increasingly concentrated in professional occupations, which do not align with the actual distribution of jobs in the labour market.
(OECD, 2025, p. 8)

Why study occupational aspirations?

An [occupational] aspiration is the single occupation named as one’s best alternative at any given time (Gottfredson, 1981, p. 548).

[A]spirations and expectations explicitly represent the ‘individual side’ of the matching process (Hillmert, 2015).

Career decisions are guided by aspirations (wishes and expectations).

  • link between social origins and destination (Sewell et al., 1957, 1969)
  • motivational function (Graf et al., 2026)
  • Mismatch between aspirations and training options hampers transitions (Jaik & Wolter, 2019).
  • Mismatch between aspirations and actual trainiong occupation reduces success
    (Beckmann et al., 2023; Fischer-Browne, 2022).

Sociological perspectives on occupational aspirations

  • Career choice as an individual, longitudinal process
  • Central question: How are aspirations shaped by social context factors?
    • gendered aspirations, gender-typing of occupations
    • social inequality of aspirations, influences of significant others - parental and peer expectations
    • influences of institutions, neighborhoods…
  • However, change in social and economic contexts are rarely studied.

Question of stability and change?

Framework of life-course sociology (Mayer, 2009; Schoon, 2012)

Decisions under conditions of societal change

Social, economic, and institutional contexts change with societal shifts:

  • educational expansion and institutional reforms
  • automation, digitalization, transition to climate-neutral economy
  • demographic change (large cohorts exiting the labor market)
  • changing norms / values

Research gap

How do changes in social, economic, and institutional contexts influence adolescents’ occupational aspirations?

  • Do students perceive changing opportunity structures in the education system and the labor market and adjust their plans;
    or is structural change purely a matter of selection by firms and educational institutions? (cf. Blossfeld, 1989).
  • Limited research that focuses on cohort changes in aspirations (cf. Schoon, 2012; Hoff et al., 2022).

Research questions

  1. Have ambitions regarding the status of aspired occupations risen?
    • How do de-tracking reforms (transition from a three-tier to a two-tier school system) affect the status of aspired occupations?
    • Which role do families play in the status increase of occupational aspirations?
    • Have inequalities in aspirations changed?
  2. Are changes in the labor market related to occupational aspirations?
    • Are occupations aspired to more often when labor market demand rises?
  3. How has the discrepancy between labor market demand and aspirations changed?
    • What is the contribution of the effects in (1) and (2)?

The German case

Stratified school system

Early between-school tracking sets a clear signal of abilities and opportunities.
( Bol & van de Werfhorst, 2013; Buchmann & Dalton, 2002; Buchmann & Park, 2009)

  • Academic track preparing for higher education (Gymnasium)
  • Medium and lower secondary tracks preparing for vocational training (Realschule, Hauptschule)

Reforms during the study period:

  • De-tracking reforms or expansion of integrated schools (from 3- to 2-/4-tier systems)
  • Expansion of pathways to the HE entrance qualification (Abitur) beyond the Gymnasium

Vocational orientation in upper secondary education

Widespread (dual) vocational training; highly standardized training certificates

  • Close link between trained and practiced occupation; comparatively low occupational mobility over the career.
  • Training and study decisions have particularly far-reaching consequences for individual careers.
  • Cohorts as carriers of structural change

(Allmendinger, 1989; Blossfeld, 1989; Bol et al., 2019; DiPrete et al., 2017; Gangl, 2001)

Trend:

Training-place shortages in the 2000s, followed by declining demand for apprenticeships during the 2010s.

Labor market development in Germany since 2000

  • Upgrading and sectoral shift from manual to service occupations (Oesch & Piccitto, 2019)
  • High unemployment and training-place shortages in the 2000s, especially in eastern German states
  • Labor shortages in many occupations: education and care, construction, and IT and technology; expected to worsen (Bundesinstitut für Berufsbildung, 2015; Hickmann & Koneberg, 2022)

Data & Research Design

Data

Secondary data analysis, combining:

  • National supplementary 9th grader sample of PISA (Germany)
  • National Educational Panel Study (NEPS), Starting Cohorts 3 and 4, waves covering grade 9 students.

Special needs schools excluded.

Clustered sampling strategy.

Measurement of realistic occupational aspirations

PISA: “What kind of job do you expect to have when you are about 30 years old?”

NEPS: “Think about everything you know right now. What occupation will you actually have later on?”

  • Coding of occupations
    • PISA 2000-2009: ISCO-88
    • NEPS: KldB-88, KldB-2010, ISCO-88 and ISCO-08 provided
    • PISA 2015-2022: ISCO-08
    • Admin Data: KldB-88, KldB-92 or KldB-2010
  • Development of Stata package kldbrecode (Gerhardt & Kappes, 2025).
  • Manual recoding of individual occupations in cases of obvious coding inconsistencies across PISA waves.

Upgrading of occupational aspirations?

Educational expansion and upgrading of aspirations

With educational expansion, educational and occupational aspirations go up.
(US: Reynolds et al., 2006; UK: Schoon, 2010; Schoon & Polek, 2011)

  • Perceived opportunities: higher education and professional positions appear more attainable (Schoon, 2010).
  • Normalization: educational expansion shapes expectations: which educational pathways and occupations seem desirable (Schoon, 2010).

No one-way causality: rising aspirations may drive educational expansion, or both reflect labor-market change, and rising returns to education.
(Becker & Mayer, 2019; Breen et al., 2009; Schoon, 2012)

Tracking and upgrading of aspirations

Track placement sends a clear signal of abilities and opportunities, and thus influences which educational and career goals seem realistic or attainable, or are expected based on the current placement.
( Bol & van de Werfhorst, 2013; Buchmann & Dalton, 2002; Buchmann & Park, 2009)

  • Aspirations depend on track placement (Basler & Kriesi, 2019; Buchmann & Dalton, 2002).
  • De-tracking reforms increased educational aspirations in Germany (Bachsleitner et al., 2025; Holtmann et al., 2024).

Changing gender inequalities?

Female upgrading of occupational aspirations 2000-2022

State of research

  • Female students in different countries have long reported more ambitious occupational and educational aspirations than male students.
    (Andres et al., 1999; Ashby & Schoon, 2010; Buchmann & Dalton, 2002; Dunne et al., 1981; Howard et al., 2011; Mau & Bikos, 2000; McDaniel, 2010; Mello, 2008; Rojewski, 1995; Sikora & Saha, 2009; Watts et al., 2015)

  • Mostly cross-sectional snapshots. No longitudinal research to show when and how gender differences in occupational aspirations came about.

  • Germany, Austria and Switzerland as exceptions (Buchmann & Dalton, 2002; McDaniel, 2010)

Why do girls have stronger upgrading of aspirations?

  • Gender-specific educational expansion
  • Increase of mother’s labor market participation and occupational status
    • Maternal occupation is more important for girls’ aspirations than for boys (Jacobs et al., 2006; Korupp et al., 2002).
  • Increasing parental education levels and number of hypogamic parents (mother education > father education)
    • Male advantages in educational attainment are smaller / female advantages larger among the highly educated (Helbig, 2012; Ortiz-Gervasi, 2021).
    • Females profit more from college-educated mothers (Buchmann & DiPrete, 2006; Minello & Blossfeld, 2017).

ISEI and education increased more among mothers

Changing gender differences in all subgroups

What occupational changes lie behind the status increase?

Gendered Upgrading - summary and discussion

Formal decomposition: Most of the gender difference in trends remains unexplained by compositional changes in, or changes in returns to, background characteristics.

What are the substantial changes behind the status variables:

  • Girls more often choose „mixed gendered“ jobs.
  • Girls who would have choosen “female” VET jobs in the past, now opt for „uni“ jobs, while boys kept chosing „dual-system VET“ jobs (more attractive male-typed VET jobs).

Increasing expectations regarding female employment: decrease in desirability of „female-typed“ VET jobs (hairdresser, shop sales assistant, office clerks)?

Adaption to the market?

Labor Market Dynamics & Occupational Aspirations

Existing research focuses on:

  • spatial variation in regional labor markets, i.e., adolescents are more likely to aspire to occupations that are more frequent in their regional labor market.
    (e.g., Flohr et al., 2020; Malin & Jacob, 2019)
  • vertical trends, i.e., the rise of aspirations for high-skilled occupations.
    (e.g., Lowe & Krahn, 2000; Schoon & Polek, 2011)

Gap: Temporal link between occupation-specific changes and aspirations.

To what extent do fluctuations in occupational prevalence, wage levels, and unemployment risks translate into shifts in occupational aspirations?

Expectations

H1 - Occupational prominence:
Changes in relative size of an occupational field → likelihood of aspiration.

H2 - Job security:
Changes in unemployment risks within an occupational field → likelihood of aspiration.

H3 - Economic returns:
Changes in wage level of an occupational field → likelihood of aspiration.

Measures

Independent variables

  • share of occupation among the employed in the respondent’s region (logged)
  • occupational unemployment rate in the respondent’s region (logged)
  • occupational wage level in the respondent’s region (logged hourly wages)

Control variables

  • stratified models by gender and Gymnasium vs other school track
  • occupation#region and occupation#PISA/NEPS fixed effects

Discrete choice analysis

Do characteristics of the alternatives influence the probability of choosing one of the alternatives?

Data structure: \(J\) rows per person \(i\) and each possible occupational aspiration \(j\).

\[ P(y_{ijrt}=1) = \frac{exp(\beta′X_{jrt} + u_{jr} + v_{js})}{\sum_{k=1}^{J} exp(\beta′X_{krt} + u_{kr} + v_{ks})} \] with:

  • \(X_{jrt}\): time-varying covariates at occupation (\(j\)) - region (\(r\)) level
  • \(u_{jr}\): occupation (\(j\)) - region (\(r\)) fixed effects
  • \(v_{js}\): occupation (\(j\)) - study (PISA vs. NEPS) (\(s\)) fixed effects

Students’ occupational aspirations adapt to changes in the market

Has aspirations - labor market discrepancy changed?

Professions have always been popular…

…and the aspiration–labor market mismatch remained stable.

Conclusions

Summary of the preliminary results

  1. Ambitions regarding the status of aspired occupations have risen.
    • Changes in school composition account for much of this rise: institutional reforms translate into shifts in ambition.
    • Girls’ aspirations rose faster than boys’: overtaking boys in terms of educational requirements of aspired occupations allowed girls to catch up to boys in the earnings potential, in line with rising demand for female employment.
  2. Aspirations do respond to regional labor-market signals — occupational prevalence, wages, and unemployment risks.
    • Adolescents perceive and adapt to the opportunity structures around them.
  3. The aspiration–labor market mismatch did not change over the observation period.
    • The enduring pull toward professional occupations may reflect labor-market trends — or help drive them.

Conclusions

Individuals adjust their aspirations in response to signals from the education system, the labor market, and societal expectations — adaptation is not purely an artifact of selection by firms and universities.

Micro-level responsiveness does not necessarily translate into a reduced aggregate mismatch: individual adaptation can sustain overall stability of the mismatch between expectations and labor market.
